newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish republican accuses UK of abusing prisoner.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish republican accuses UK of abusing prisoner.

text.p: A Northern Irish republican leader on Tuesday accused Britain of 'mentally and physically' abusing a sick and heavily pregnant prisoner who is awaiting extradition to Germany.

Martin McGuinness, chief negotiator for the IRA's political arm Sinn Fein, said it was intolerable that 25-year-old Roisin McAliskey should be in prison when she is expecting her first child next week.

"To have your first child on the outside is a very, very traumatic experience and it is particularly so in my opinion when the young woman is being held in captivity," McGuinness told reporters after visiting McAliskey at London's Holloway prison.
"She (McAliskey) has been subjected to abuse of a mental and physical nature and that is intolerable."
Earlier on Tuesday, a London court ordered that McAliskey be kept in prison for another 28 days while she waits for her extradition case to be heard.

She has been held in Britain since she was arrested in Belfast last November. Germany wants her to face charges connected to an Irish Republican Army (IRA) bombing last year of a British Army base at Osnabrueck.
McAliskey was too ill to appear in court on Tuesday. Media reports say she has been confined to a wheelchair for several weeks and that her baby is dangerously small.
The prisoner is the daughter of Bernadette McAliskey, nee Devlin, a fiery Northern Irish republican who was Britain's youngest member of parliament when she took her seat in the 1960s.
Roisin McAliskey has denied any part in the Osnabrueck mortar attack in which buildings were damaged but no-one was injured.
McGuinness said there was "not one shred of evidence against McAliskey" and he urged Britain to grant her bail "pending her eventual release".
McAliskey's imprisonment has provoked outrage in Ireland and among republicans, who say she has been kept in appalling conditions and subjected to regular strip searches.
British prison authorities reduced slightly her security categorisation in March, meaning she would no longer be subject to frequent strip searches.
Irish foreign minister Dick Spring recently summoned Britain's ambassador in Dublin to protest at McAliskey's treatment.
A spokesman for Britain's prisons service denied McGuinness's charges, saying McAliskey "is being held in humane and decent conditions" and that she was receiving proper medical care.

Under the Conservative government ousted in the May 1 election, Britain agreed that McAliskey will be allowed to keep her baby and will be transferred to a special mother and baby unit in the prison after she gives birth.
McGuinness's visit to London was his first since he was elected on May 1 to the British parliament to represent the seat of mid-Ulster.
He and other Sinn Fein MP's refuse to take up their seats in the Westminster parliament because they say this would suggest they accepted Britain's right to rule Northern Ireland.
But McGuinness told Sky news that Sinn Fein was now considering opening an office at Westminster.
